docs.title: Air-gapped Zeus OS / v9s install
docs.text: For environments without outbound internet from the cluster.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Build the container image on a connected bastion, save with podman save / docker save
  2. Transfer image tarball + Helm chart + ui/dist bundle to the air-gap zone
  3. Import image into cluster containerd (ctr images import on k3s)

docs.title: Configure engines offline
docs.text:
Set explicit URLs — auto-discovery will not reach node IPs outside the enclave:

config:
  transivaUrl: "https://engines.internal:5080"
  hyper2kvmUrl: "https://engines.internal:5070"
  guestkitUrl: "https://engines.internal:5092"
  packetwolfHost: "packetwolf.internal"
  packetwolfTls: true

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
./scripts/deploy-remote.sh AIRGAP_HOST admin --k3s --skip-cluster-prereqs

Skip --ui-pages-e2e if Playwright cannot run from your workstation.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n zeus-os
curl -k https://AIRGAP_HOST:30050/api/v1/health
python3 scripts/e2e-remediation-audit.py https://AIRGAP_HOST:30050

PacketWolf and migration engines are optional — v9s day-2 centers degrade gracefully when engines are unreachable.

docs.title: Content library: signed template bundles between Zeus instances
docs.text:
The content library moves VM templates from one Zeus instance to another as a single signed JSON file (a bundle). It is opt-in, additive and conservative: nothing is ever auto-approved, nothing existing is overwritten, and a bundle is only accepted when it is signed by a key you have chosen to trust.

Existing git sync (POST /templates/sync-git) is unchanged and independent.

docs.title: What a bundle contains
docs.text:
{
  "format_version": 1,
  "kind": "zeus-template-bundle",
  "bundle_id": "bundle-<uuid>",
  "created_at": "2026-09-25T12:00:00+00:00",
  "source_instance": { "id": "<key id>", "name": "lab-a" },
  "templates": [
    {
      "name": "web-base", "display_name": "...", "description": "...",
      "category": "linux", "os_type": "linux", "version": "1.2.0",
      "tags": [], "quick_deploy": false,
      "spec": { "...": "cpu, memory, disk, cloud_init, ..." },
      "parameters": [],
      "source_status": "approved",
      "executable_content": ["spec.cloud_init"],
      "omitted_fields": ["spec.storage_class"],
      "sha256": "<hex sha-256 of this template's canonical JSON>"
    }
  ],
  "signature": { "alg": "ed25519", "key_id": "...", "public_key": "<base64>", "value": "<base64>" }
}
  • executable_content flags the members that run code inside a guest. Today that is spec.cloud_init. The importer recomputes it and never trusts the flag.
  • Instance-local references are stripped on export and listed in omitted_fields: spec.golden_datavolume, spec.storage_class, and the default value of any secret parameter. Storage class names inside additional_disks and network attachment names are kept but are not verified against the importing cluster; they may need editing after import.
  • Only ConfigMap-backed templates are exported (the same ones GET /templates shows as source: configmap). Built-in and golden templates are not.

docs.title: Trust model (read this)
docs.text:
Signatures use Ed25519, so verification needs only a public key.

  • Each instance generates a signing key on first use and stores it in $ZEUS_OS_DATA_DIR/template-library-signing-key.json with mode 0600. It is never returned by the API or logged. If the file exists but is unreadable the export fails; the key is never silently regenerated (that would change the instance's identity and break every peer that pinned it). Back this file up along with the rest of the data dir; losing it means peers must re-pin a new key.
  • GET /templates/library/key returns the public key and its key id (first 16 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the raw key).
  • A signature only proves the bundle was made by some key. It is accepted only if that key is one of:
  • this instance's own key (lets you re-import your own bundle),
  • a key pinned by a visible subscription,
  • a key listed in ZEUS_OS_LIBRARY_TRUSTED_KEYS (comma separated <base64> or <label>=<base64>).

An unsigned bundle, a bundle signed by an unknown key, or a bundle that embeds a different key than the one you trust is rejected. The embedded signature.public_key is never trusted on its own. * When you import from a subscription, only that subscription's pinned key is accepted, not the wider trust set. * Key pinning at subscribe time. POST /templates/library/subscribe takes an optional public_key. If you supply it, that is what gets pinned. If you omit it the server fetches /templates/library/key from the remote once and pins the result (trust on first use). The response then carries a warning and the fingerprint: confirm it with the remote operator over another channel. Anyone able to intercept that first fetch could substitute their own key, so prefer supplying the key when the channel is not fully trusted. * Verification does not protect against a trusted peer that ships bad content. That is why imports are drafts (below).

What is covered by the signature: the canonical serialisation (keys sorted, 4.0 and 4 equal, no insignificant whitespace) of the whole manifest minus the signature member. Changing any template, hash, bundle_id, timestamp or source name invalidates it. Each template also carries its own SHA-256, checked as a second layer.

docs.title: Import policy
docs.text:
POST /templates/library/import (Editor or Admin):

Rule Behaviour Status Every imported template is draft, whatever source_status says. Approving is a separate, normal step. Drafts cannot be deployed to production namespaces, and elsewhere only when ZEUS_OS_ALLOW_DRAFT_TEMPLATES=1. Ownership Created as ConfigMaps in the namespace you name (default default); tenant scope is enforced with the same namespace check as POST /templates. The namespace must already exist. Overwrite Never. A name that exists in the target namespace, or that matches a built-in template (a same-named ConfigMap would shadow it), is skipped (on_conflict: "skip", the default) or imported as <name>-imported, -imported-2, ... ("rename"). Creation uses Kubernetes create, so a race also cannot overwrite. Validation Each template goes through build_configmap_from_save, the same code as POST /templates (cloud-init security scan, denylist, 128 KiB cloud-init cap), plus DNS-label names, label-safe category/os_type/tags, and numeric bounds (1-512 vCPU, memory up to 4096 GiB, disk up to 64 TiB). Invalid entries are reported and skipped; the rest still import. Caps 4 MiB per bundle, 512 KiB per template, 200 templates, 50 subscriptions. Fetches stop reading at the cap. Executable content A real import of any template with cloud-init requires "acknowledge_executable_content": true, otherwise the request is refused with 400. Dry-run does not require it. Dry run "dry_run": true verifies everything and returns the per-template plan without creating anything. Audit Every export, subscribe, unsubscribe and real import is written to the remediation audit (template_library.*), including rejected bundles (bad signature, unknown signer, failed fetch).

Imported ConfigMaps carry the labels/annotations zeus-os.io/imported=true, zeus-os.io/library-bundle-id, -source-instance, -signer-key-id, -content-sha256, -source-name, zeus-os.io/imported-by, zeus-os.io/imported-at, and zeus-os.io/author: library-import.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
All under /api/v1.

Method and path Role Purpose GET /templates/library any authenticated user Signed bundle of the templates the caller can see. Query: namespace, status, names (comma separated). Tenant scope is the same as GET /templates. GET /templates/library/key any authenticated user {algorithm, key_id, public_key, format_version, instance_name} GET /templates/library/subscriptions any authenticated user Subscriptions visible to the caller's tenant. Tokens are never returned (has_token only). POST /templates/library/subscribe Admin {name, url, token?, public_key?} DELETE /templates/library/subscriptions/{id} Admin Removes the subscription and its pinned key (owner tenant enforced). POST /templates/library/import Editor+ {namespace, bundle \| subscription_id, dry_run, on_conflict, acknowledge_executable_content}

A template literally named key in a namespace named library is shadowed on GET /templates/library/key by the static route; use another name.

docs.title: Outbound fetch and SSRF guard
docs.text:
Subscriptions are fetched by the server, so the URL is treated as hostile. The rules match the plugin registry:

  • https only, unless ZEUS_OS_LIBRARY_ALLOW_HTTP=1.
  • No credentials in the URL, no query string or fragment on the base URL.
  • Loopback, private, link-local (including 169.254.169.254), CGNAT, unique-local and multicast addresses, single-label hosts and .local/.internal/.svc/.cluster.local/.lan names are refused unless the exact host is listed in ZEUS_OS_LIBRARY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS (comma separated).
  • The hostname is resolved by the server, every address is checked, and the connection is pinned to the checked addresses (defeats DNS rebinding).
  • Redirects are not followed. 15 second timeout. Body capped while streaming.

The subscription bearer token is stored in $ZEUS_OS_DATA_DIR/template-library-subscriptions.json (mode 0600) in clear text, like other integration credentials in the JSON stores. Use a token with the least privilege that can read templates on the remote.

Subscriptions are tenant-scoped through owner_tenant: a subscription created by a tenant-scoped admin is visible (and its key trusted) only for that tenant; one created by a platform admin is shared.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Purpose ZEUS_OS_LIBRARY_ALLOW_HTTP 1 allows plain http:// subscription URLs (default off). ZEUS_OS_LIBRARY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS Exact hosts exempt from the internal-address block. ZEUS_OS_LIBRARY_TRUSTED_KEYS Extra trusted public keys (<base64> or <label>=<base64>), for uploaded bundles from instances you do not subscribe to. ZEUS_OS_INSTANCE_NAME Human-readable name put in source_instance.name (default zeus-os).

docs.title: UI
docs.text: Templates, then Content library: download a signed bundle, import from a file or a subscription, and manage subscriptions (admins). An import is always previewed first. When any template carries cloud-init the sheet shows a warning and the confirm button stays disabled until the acknowledgement box is ticked.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• The template list caches ConfigMaps for 30 seconds, so an import can take up to that long to appear in GET /templates.
  • There is no bundle revocation or key rotation flow. To rotate, delete the key file on the exporter (a new key is generated on next use) and re-pin it on every peer.
  • Version numbers inside a bundle are informational; there is no dependency resolution between templates.

docs.title: Email (SMTP) notification channel
docs.text:
Zeus OS can deliver notifications by email through any SMTP relay. Email is a regular notification channel type (email) next to Slack, Teams, generic webhook and PagerDuty, so it works everywhere a channel does: the Notifications page, POST /api/v1/notifications/channels/{id}/test, POST /api/v1/notifications/send, and the shortcut notify action.

Nothing is sent until an operator creates a channel. There is no default relay, no default credentials, and tests never contact a real mail server.

docs.title: Channel config
docs.text:
Create the channel with channel_type: "email" and this config:

Field Required Meaning host yes SMTP relay hostname or IP port no Defaults from security (starttls 587, tls 465, none 25) security no starttls (default, upgrade is mandatory), tls (implicit TLS), none (plaintext) username with password SMTP AUTH user password one of the two SMTP AUTH password, stored in the channel config, write-only (masked on read) password_env one of the two Name of an environment variable on the Zeus OS server holding the password; keeps the secret out of the JSON store. Not masked (it is a name, not a secret) from yes zeus@example.com or Zeus OS <zeus@example.com> to yes List of addresses (a comma/semicolon/newline separated string is also accepted); at most 20, duplicates removed subject_prefix no Prepended to the subject, e.g. [prod] 
{
  "name": "ops-email",
  "channel_type": "email",
  "config": {
    "host": "smtp.example.com", "port": 587, "security": "starttls",
    "username": "alerts", "password_env": "ZEUS_OS_SMTP_PASSWORD",
    "from": "Zeus OS <zeus@example.com>",
    "to": ["ops@example.com", "oncall@example.com"],
    "subject_prefix": "[prod]"
  }
}

Validation happens at create/update time (no network): bad hosts, ports, addresses, an empty recipient list, more than 20 recipients, both password and password_env, a username without a password (or vice versa), and credentials with security: none (credentials are never sent in plaintext) are rejected with a 400 that names the problem.

docs.title: The message
docs.text:
A multipart/alternative message with a plain-text part and a simple HTML part: [SEVERITY] title, the message body, and severity / source / time / metadata.

  • Subject and all header fields have CR, LF and every other control character stripped (header injection), and are length-capped.
  • Everything user-controlled is HTML-escaped in the HTML part.
  • The body is capped at 32 KiB ([message truncated] is appended); at most 50 metadata entries are included.
  • Addresses are parsed strictly; addresses containing control characters are rejected rather than "cleaned".

docs.title: Honest delivery reporting
docs.text:
ok is true only when the SMTP server accepts the message (2xx reply to DATA). status_code is the SMTP reply code (e.g. 250); the test endpoint also returns "protocol": "SMTP". A rejected recipient (550), failed login (535), TLS failure, timeout, blocked host, or unset password_env variable is ok: false with the reason in error, and is recorded in the notification history as failed. Passwords never appear in errors, logs or API responses.

Timeouts: 10 s per SMTP command/connect, 40 s for the whole exchange.

docs.title: Security posture (SSRF)
docs.text:
Same posture as the webhook channels:

  • The relay host is resolved, every returned address is checked, and the connection goes to the checked IP (defeats DNS rebinding). TLS certificates are still verified against the configured hostname (webpki roots, rustls; no native-tls).
  • Loopback, link-local (cloud metadata), private (RFC 1918/ULA), carrier-grade NAT, multicast/unspecified addresses and localhost, *.local, *.svc, *.cluster.local, *.internal names are refused.
  • Only ports 25, 465, 587 and 2525 are accepted.

Operator switches (environment of the Zeus OS server; safe defaults are off):

Variable Effect ZEUS_OS_SMTP_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1 Also permit RFC 1918 / ULA relay addresses and in-cluster hostnames (mail.mail.svc). Loopback, link-local/metadata and CGNAT stay blocked. ZEUS_OS_SMTP_EXTRA_PORTS=2526,1025 Additional allowed SMTP ports

Creating or editing channels needs the Editor role; sending a test needs Editor as well. Channels are tenant-scoped like every other channel.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
web/src/notification_dispatch.rs contains an in-process fake SMTP server (tokio TcpListener speaking EHLO/MAIL/RCPT/DATA/QUIT on 127.0.0.1) used to verify the recipients and body actually received, and the failure path when the server rejects a recipient:

cargo test -p zeus-os-web --bins notification_dispatch

For a manual check against a real relay, create the channel in the UI and press Test on its card; the result shows the SMTP reply code or the real error.

docs.title: Zeus OS features
docs.text:
Every feature in the current product, one by one: 146 features across 19 groups. Features marked Preview or Partial have documented limits, stated in the row; unknown values are shown as unknown, never as zero.

  • 1. VM Lifecycle & Fleet Operations
  • 2. Consoles & Remote Access
  • 3. Networking & PacketWolf VM Shield
  • 4. Storage & Data
  • 5. Cost, FinOps & Optimization
  • 6. Capacity, Autoscaling & Placement
  • 7. Observability, Topology & Time Machine
  • 8. Security Posture & Vulnerability
  • 9. Compliance, Governance & Admission Control
  • 10. Day-2 Automation & Remediation
  • 11. Incident Response & War Room
  • 12. GitOps, CI/CD & Change Management
  • 13. Backup, DR & Snapshots
  • 14. Multi-Cluster, Multi-Tenancy & Enterprise Identity
  • 15. AI Ops, Marketplace & Developer Center
  • 16. Edge, Chaos, Performance & Platform Ops
  • Also included

docs.title: 1. VM Lifecycle & Fleet Operations
docs.text:
Create, run, migrate, and manage KubeVirt virtual machines at fleet scale without touching kubectl.

Feature What it does VM Command Center Browse, filter, and operate every KubeVirt VM and running instance from one inventory with power, pause, restart, and detail drill-down. VM Workbench & Power Actions Start, stop, restart, pause, and delete VMs from a dedicated workbench separated from read-only browse views. VM Setup & Template Wizard Guided creation from instance types, preferences, and templates with cluster-grounded, AI-assisted manifest generation. Templates & Instance Type Catalog Curated VM templates, KubeVirt instance types, and preferences browsable and one-click deployable. Hot-Plug CPU, Memory & Disks Add vCPU, RAM, and data disks to running VMs live without a reboot. NIC Model Selection Choose VirtIO or e1000e per network interface, at creation or on an existing VM. Virtual Devices & Memory Overcommit Toggle watchdog, VirtIO RNG, sound, USB tablet, serial console, and the virtio memory-balloon device per VM. Live Migration Assistant Preview Plan and start live VM migrations with a guided wizard. Some pre-checks are estimates and the target node is not yet passed to KubeVirt. Migration Factory Partial Batch-migrate and convert VMs, including disk conversion, across nodes and storage as a supervised campaign. Cross-cluster migration is not implemented yet. VM Groups & Fleet Bulk Ops Organize VMs into logical groups and apply power, tagging, and lifecycle actions in bulk. VM Clone & Compare Clone VMs from running state or snapshots and diff two VMs' configuration side by side. VM Health & Repair Per-VM health scoring plus guided repair actions for stuck, unschedulable, or degraded instances. Windows Enterprise & Licensing Windows guest customization, sysprep, and license tracking for Windows VM estates. Windows via Kryton Optional Kryton REST catalog for Windows create + golden factory (12 dockur IDs); Zeus keeps day-2 VNC/native RDP/GuestKit. Guest Intelligence Reads guest-agent data for OS, IPs, installed software, and in-guest state.

docs.title: 2. Consoles & Remote Access
docs.text:
Live VNC, serial, terminal, RDP, and SSH access with real-time metrics — all in the browser.

Feature What it does VNC Graphical Console Full graphical VM console streamed over WebSocket, including a pop-out standalone window. Serial Console Live serial-port console for headless VMs and boot-time troubleshooting. Native RDP & SSH (NodePort expose) One-click expose of RDP or SSH over a NodePort (a free port is assigned and collisions are rejected), then connect with your own client using a downloadable .rdp file or an ssh command. Console Hub & Workspace Multi-console workspace with tabs, session management, and a unified console launcher. Live Console Metrics Real-time CPU, memory, disk, and network telemetry streamed alongside each console. Console Session Recording & Sharing Record, replay, and share console sessions for training, audit, and collaboration. In-Browser Terminal Cluster and pod terminal access with WebSocket-backed shells.

docs.title: 3. Networking & PacketWolf VM Shield
docs.text:
See exactly what a VM talks to and contain it in one click — kernel-native visibility and enforcement.

Feature What it does PacketWolf VM Shield Unified per-VM network visibility and one-click containment with desired-vs-actual verification and a background reconciler. Live Flow Watch (Hubble) Streams a VM's live allowed/denied flows, dependency map, public-exposure findings, and an explainable risk score. Containment Profiles Internet lock, full quarantine, lateral lock, exfiltration lock, and investigation mode — with optional termination of existing connections. Policy Preview & Dry-Run Dry-runs the exact containment policy against recorded traffic to show what it will and won't break. Per-VM Firewall & Egress Control Block specific outbound ports (SMB, RDP, C2) and manage per-VM firewall rules from a panel. Cilium Dashboard Visualize Cilium identities, endpoints, and network policy enforcement across the cluster. Network Policy Builder Visually author, simulate, and apply Kubernetes and Cilium network policies. Network Flow & Observability Cluster-wide network flow maps, attachments (Multus), and traffic observability. Service Mesh & Ingress Manage service mesh routing, ingress rules, service discovery, and full MetalLB IPAddressPool/L2Advertisement CRUD (create and delete pools, not just view). VM-Aware Ingress Create, validate, and delete Ingress rules for a VM's exposed Service directly from the VM inspector, with TLS-secret and host-conflict checks before you apply. Host Networking (NMState) Declare NIC/bond/VLAN configuration for cluster nodes and see per-node apply status, via the kubernetes-nmstate operator. DNS & IPAM Cluster DNS records and IP address management for VMs and services.

docs.title: 4. Storage & Data
docs.text:
Manage DataVolumes, disks, PVCs, images, and storage migration for the whole VM estate.

Feature What it does Storage Explorer Unified view of storage classes, PVCs, volumes, and capacity across the cluster. DataVolumes & CDI Import Create and import DataVolumes from URLs, registries, and uploads via the CDI upload flow. Disk Manager & Hot-Plug Add, resize, and hot-plug VM disks including live PVC resize. Image Library, Factory & Registry Curate boot images, build images with the Image Factory (Zeus ISO pipelines and optional Build with Kryton), and browse the image registry. Storage Migration Move VM volumes between storage classes and backends with supervised migration. Volume Snapshots Point-in-time volume snapshots integrated with the snapshot manager. Storage Intelligence Analytics on storage usage, waste, and growth trends with optimization hints. Atlas Distributed Storage Read-only Ceph/NFS backend, cluster, and pool inventory proxied from Atlas (the Zyvor storage control plane), surfaced on the Storage page.

docs.title: 5. Cost, FinOps & Optimization
docs.text:
Per-VM cost visibility, waste detection, forecasting, chargeback, and rightsizing.

Feature What it does Cost Intelligence Dashboard Partial Per-VM and per-namespace cost from a price model you configure, with trends and drill-down. A model, not billing data. Chargeback & Cost Allocation Allocate spend to tenants, teams, and projects with a chargeback engine and reports. Waste Detection & Rightsizing Finds idle, oversized, and orphaned resources and recommends right-sized shapes. Cost Forecasting Projects future spend from usage trends and growth models. Budget Alerts Server-side monthly budgets per cluster, tenant or namespace, evaluated from recorded cost history, with one alert per threshold per month through your notification channels. Estimates from configured unit prices, not invoices. Spot & Savings Advisor Identifies spot and savings-plan opportunities for eligible workloads. Optimization Center Consolidated hub of cost, capacity, and performance optimization recommendations. Cost Estimator Pre-deployment cost estimation for planned VMs and workloads.

docs.title: 6. Capacity, Autoscaling & Placement
docs.text:
Plan headroom, schedule smartly, and scale nodes, pods, and VMs automatically.

Feature What it does Capacity Planning Cluster and node capacity dashboards with headroom, saturation, and what-if analysis. Cluster Autoscaling Configure and observe node autoscaling behavior and scale events. HPA & VPA Managers Manage Horizontal and Vertical Pod Autoscalers with recommendations. Placement Advisor Recommends optimal nodes for VMs using affinity, taints, and resource fit. Affinity, Taints & Tolerations Author affinity/anti-affinity rules, node taints, and tolerations visually. Priority & Runtime Classes Manage PriorityClasses, RuntimeClasses, and Pod Disruption Budgets. Utilization Heatmap Cluster-wide heatmap of resource pressure across nodes and namespaces. Node & HA/DRS Management Node inventory, cordon/drain, and HA/DRS workload balancing, from suggest-only to fully automated, with a per-VM cooldown against thrashing and a full history of what the engine moved and why. Manual Node Fencing Force-remediate a node you have confirmed dead out of band: cordon it and force-delete its VM instances so KubeVirt reschedules them elsewhere. Needs an explicit opt-in and a "node is dead" confirmation, and refuses on any node still reporting Ready. GPU & Device Plugins Manage GPU dashboards, device plugins, and hardware device attachment, including a vGPU mediated-device profile picker with a manual-resource fallback when no GPU hardware is present.

docs.title: 7. Observability, Topology & Time Machine
docs.text:
Topology maps, distributed tracing, logs, metrics, and point-in-time cluster history.

Feature What it does Topology & Dependency Graph Interactive maps of nodes, VMs, pods, services, and their dependencies. Cluster DVR & VM Flight Recorder Time Machine that continuously samples cluster and per-VM state for point-in-time replay. Distributed Tracing & APM Partial Service list, request rate and error rate from PacketWolf flows. Latency percentiles are shown only when measured, otherwise unknown. Logs Explorer & Aggregation Centralized log search and aggregation across pods and VMs. Metrics & Custom Metrics Real Prometheus-backed metrics, custom metric dashboards, and monitoring targets. Anomaly Detection Detects abnormal resource, cost, and behavior patterns automatically. Timeline & Gantt View Partial Chronological timeline of events and remediation actions, and Gantt-style operation views. Event Analysis Correlates and analyzes Kubernetes events for root-cause signals. System Health & Status Page Overall cluster health scoring and a shareable status page.

docs.title: 8. Security Posture & Vulnerability
docs.text:
Continuous posture scoring, image scanning, secrets, and a dedicated security operations center.

Feature What it does Security Posture & Overview Continuous scoring of cluster and VM security posture with prioritized findings. Vulnerability & Image Scanning Scans container and VM images for CVEs with severity breakdowns. Security Operations Center Consolidated SecOps view of threats, containment actions, and response state. Secrets & External Secrets Manage Kubernetes secrets and External Secrets Operator integrations. Certificate Manager Track, issue, and rotate TLS certificates across the cluster. eBPF & Kernel Intelligence Kernel-level (eBPF) runtime signals and kernel info for deep security context. Patch Center Partial Patch readiness checks and patch planning. Zeus OS does not execute patches yet.

docs.title: 9. Compliance, Governance & Admission Control
docs.text:
Frameworks, policy engines, admission webhooks, and RBAC visualization for provable control.

Feature What it does Compliance & Frameworks Continuous compliance checks mapped to frameworks with pass/fail evidence. OPA Gatekeeper & Zeus Policies Manage OPA Gatekeeper constraints and native Zeus policy definitions. Admission Control Configure admission webhooks and validate resources before they're admitted. Policy Simulation & Violations Simulate policy impact and track live policy violations. RBAC Visualizer Visual map of roles, bindings, service accounts, and effective permissions. Audit Log & Trail Immutable audit trail of every action across surfaces. Resource Governance & Quotas Resource quotas, limits, and governance policy across namespaces and tenants. Resource Tagging Consistent tagging and labeling for ownership, cost, and policy.

docs.title: 10. Day-2 Automation & Remediation
docs.text:
Closed-loop remediation, scheduled operations, workflows, and macros that run the boring parts.

Feature What it does Day-2 Closed-Loop Remediation Background engine that detects signals and runs remediation playbooks with a kill-switch. Auto-Remediation Playbooks Registry of remediation playbooks with signal-to-action mapping and audit. Scheduled Operations Schedule power on/off, snapshots, and other operations on cron-like cadences. Workflow Automation & Manager Compose multi-step operational workflows across resources. Macros & Batch Actions Preview Bulk operations across many resources. Macro recording and replay is not yet available. Task Center Central queue of running, scheduled, and completed operational tasks. Undo & Rollback Rollback and undo support for reversible operations.

docs.title: 11. Incident Response & War Room
docs.text:
Auto-assembled war rooms, guided response wizards, RCA, and SLA/SLO tracking.

Feature What it does Incident Center Track active incidents with severity, timeline, and correlated context. War Room Auto-Assembly Automatically assembles topology, logs, metrics, and RCA context for an active incident. Incident Response Wizard Guided, step-by-step response flows with recommended remediation. Incident Chat In-context collaboration thread tied to an incident. SLA Dashboard & SLO Manager Define and track SLOs, error budgets, and SLA compliance. Alerting & Notifications Alert rules, Prometheus rules, notification routing, and an alerting engine. Executive Briefing Auto-generated briefings summarizing state, risk, and incidents for leadership.

docs.title: 12. GitOps, CI/CD & Change Management
docs.text:
Argo/Flux sync, Helm and Kustomize, progressive delivery, and gated change approval.

Feature What it does GitOps Sync (Argo/Flux) Partial Read-only view of Flux and Argo CD sync state and drift for objects that already exist in the cluster. Helm & Kustomize Browse and manage Helm releases and Kustomize overlays. Progressive Delivery Canary, blue-green, and progressive rollout strategies with health gating. CI/CD Pipelines View and integrate CI/CD pipeline status for delivered workloads. Change Approval & Approvals Gate risky changes behind approval workflows before they execute. Infrastructure as Code Manage IaC definitions and environment configuration for the estate. Environment Management Model and manage dev/stage/prod environments and promotion.

docs.title: 13. Backup, DR & Snapshots
docs.text:
Velero-backed backups, disaster recovery orchestration, and scheduled VM snapshots.

Feature What it does Backup & DR Center Configure and monitor VM/cluster backups with a guided backup wizard. Velero Integration Native Velero backup and restore management for Kubernetes and VM resources. Disaster Recovery Orchestration Partial DR plans with measured RPO and a real restore test into a scratch namespace. Failover and execute steps are simulated and labelled as such. Fleet-wide operations, tenant isolation, OIDC/LDAP/SAML/MFA, API tokens, and SIEM.

docs.title: SCIM 2.0 provisioning
docs.text:
Zeus OS exposes a SCIM 2.0 (RFC 7643 / RFC 7644) server so an identity provider can create, update, deactivate and delete users and groups. It is mounted at /scim/v2 (not under /api/v1) and is disabled by default: every path answers 404 until it is configured.

Implementation: web/src/scim.rs (protocol and semantics), web/src/routes/scim.rs (HTTP layer and bearer middleware), storage in the local auth user store (ZEUS_OS_LOCAL_USERS_FILE) plus scim-groups.json in ZEUS_OS_DATA_DIR.

docs.title: Enabling
docs.text:
Variable Purpose ZEUS_OS_SCIM_TOKEN Static provisioning bearer token. Minimum 32 characters; a shorter value is rejected (SCIM stays disabled and an error is logged). Generate one with openssl rand -hex 32. ZEUS_OS_SCIM_API_TOKEN_AUTH 1/true: also accept a Zeus API token (v9s_...) that belongs to an admin and carries the admin scope. Off by default. ZEUS_OS_SCIM off disables SCIM even if a token is configured (kill-switch). ZEUS_OS_SCIM_GROUP_ADMIN Comma-separated group displayNames that grant the platform-wide admin role. Empty by default: no group grants admin unless you list it here. ZEUS_OS_SCIM_GROUP_EDITOR Group names granting editor (default zeus-os-editors). ZEUS_OS_SCIM_GROUP_VIEWER Group names granting viewer (default zeus-os-viewers). ZEUS_OS_SCIM_TENANT_GROUP_PREFIX Prefix of tenant groups (default zeus-os-tenant-).

The SCIM base URL is https://<zeus-host>/scim/v2.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Every request needs Authorization: Bearer <token>. SCIM has its own middleware and never accepts a normal Zeus user session (Authorization header, cookie, query string or WebSocket sub-protocol): a valid admin session gets 401. The static token is compared in constant time (SHA-256 digests). Responses: 404 = SCIM not enabled, 401 = missing/wrong token, 403 = an API token that is not an admin token with the admin scope.

The token is a powerful credential: whoever holds it can create users and place them in groups. Treat it like an admin password, rotate it by changing the environment variable and restarting, and prefer a network policy that only allows your IdP to reach /scim/v2. If you list a group in ZEUS_OS_SCIM_GROUP_ADMIN, the token holder can create platform admins by adding a user to that group; only do so deliberately.

docs.title: What is (and is not) provisioned
docs.text:
• SCIM manages local accounts in the Zeus user store. Only accounts created through SCIM are visible to or modifiable by SCIM. The built-in break-glass admin and any user created manually (Settings or /api/v1/auth/users) are unreachable: they are not listed, GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE /Users/{id} returns 404 for them, they cannot be group members, and their user names are reserved. Creating a SCIM user whose userName matches an existing account (case-insensitively) returns 409; admin, api_key and dev return 403.
  • Passwords are never accepted or returned. A password attribute (POST/PUT/PATCH) is rejected with 400 invalidValue. changePassword is reported as unsupported. A provisioned user has no local password, so local login (/auth/login) fails for them; an administrator can still set a local password with the existing user-management API, after which they can log in locally as well. Sign-in for SCIM users is intended to be via your SSO.
  • JIT users are out of scope. Users that OIDC/SAML/LDAP create on first login are not SCIM users and are not affected. Note that, in this release, SSO session creation does not consult the SCIM active flag: SCIM deactivation revokes the user's existing Zeus sessions, OIDC sessions and API tokens (by user name) and blocks local login, but an IdP-side deactivation is what stops new SSO logins. A helper (local_auth::is_scim_deactivated) exists for wiring a deny check into the SSO login paths.
  • A newly provisioned user is a viewer until a mapped group says otherwise.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Supported attributes: userName (1-128 ASCII characters: letters, digits, _ - . @ +, starting with a letter or digit; e-mail style names are fine), externalId, displayName, name.givenName, name.familyName, emails (one address is stored: the primary one, else the first), active. groups is read-only. Other core attributes (for example phoneNumbers, title, roles) and the enterprise extension are accepted and ignored. roles are ignored on purpose: access comes only from groups. Some IdPs send booleans as the strings "True" / "False"; both forms are accepted.

active: false (via PUT or PATCH):

  1. marks the user inactive (local login refused),
  2. revokes all their Zeus sessions and OIDC sessions,
  3. revokes their API tokens.

DELETE removes the user, removes them from all groups and revokes the same credentials. A PUT that omits active leaves it unchanged (it cannot silently re-enable a deactivated user). Renaming (userName change) revokes the credentials issued under the old name.

docs.title: Groups and role / tenant mapping
docs.text:
Groups are stored by Zeus; membership is by SCIM user id. A group's displayName (case-insensitive, exact match) decides what it grants:

displayName Effect listed in ZEUS_OS_SCIM_GROUP_ADMIN member gets the admin role. As for local admins this is platform-wide (no tenant list). Nothing is listed by default. listed in ZEUS_OS_SCIM_GROUP_EDITOR (default zeus-os-editors) editor listed in ZEUS_OS_SCIM_GROUP_VIEWER (default zeus-os-viewers) viewer <prefix><tenant-id> (default zeus-os-tenant-acme) member belongs to tenant acme (namespace label zeus-os.io/tenant). <tenant-id> must be 1-63 characters of A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ . anything else stored, but grants nothing

A user's effective role is the highest role among their groups (default viewer); tenants are the union of their tenant groups. A non-admin with no tenant group keeps the default scope (a tenant named after their user name). Whenever membership, a group name, or the mapping changes, the access of every SCIM-managed user is recomputed on the next SCIM write; users whose role/tenants changed have their sessions revoked (a session is a snapshot of the old role) and an audit entry is written. Deleting a group demotes its members accordingly. Nested groups are not supported; group members must be SCIM user ids that exist.

docs.title: Filtering, pagination, PATCH
docs.text:
• GET /Users and GET /Groups accept filter, startIndex (1-based), count (default 100, max 200; count=0 returns only totalResults). sortBy, attributes and excludedAttributes are ignored.
  • Filter operators: eq ne co sw ew pr, combined with and, or, not(...) and parentheses. gt/ge/lt/le are rejected (400 invalidFilter). Filterable attributes: users id externalId userName displayName active emails.value name.givenName name.familyName; groups id externalId displayName members.value. id and externalId compare case-exactly, other strings case-insensitively.
  • PATCH supports add, replace, remove, with or without path. Paths may be schema-qualified (urn:...:User:userName), dotted (name.givenName) or use a value filter (emails[type eq "work"].value, members[value eq "<id>"]). On groups, members supports add, replace, remove-all, remove by filter and remove by value list. A PATCH is atomic: if any operation fails nothing is applied.
  • Not supported (advertised as such in /ServiceProviderConfig): bulk, sort, ETags, change-password.
  • Errors use the SCIM error schema with application/scim+json.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text: Every mutation is written through the auth audit log (auth-audit.jsonl, SIEM export) with the caller as subject (scim for the static token, scim:<subject> for an API token) and only the userName / group displayName as detail: scim_user_created, scim_user_updated, scim_user_deactivated, scim_user_reactivated, scim_user_deleted, scim_group_created, scim_group_updated, scim_group_members_changed, scim_group_deleted, scim_access_changed (role/tenant changed, with the new role). Tokens and e-mail addresses are never logged. Failed authentication is logged to the server log only (not the audit file) so unauthenticated callers cannot grow it.

docs.title: Configuring an IdP
docs.text:
Generic SCIM 2.0 client settings: base URL https://<zeus-host>/scim/v2, authentication "HTTP header / bearer token" with the value of ZEUS_OS_SCIM_TOKEN, unique identifier field userName. This server has been tested against its own automated test-suite only, not against live Okta or Entra ID tenants, and this page does not reproduce vendor UI steps or vendor behaviour claims. What to check in whichever IdP you use:

  • Okta (SCIM 2.0 app integration) and Microsoft Entra ID (enterprise application provisioning) both offer a generic SCIM 2.0 mode with bearer-token authentication: point it at the base URL and paste the token.
  • Enable create / update / deactivate actions; leave password sync off (a password is rejected with 400).
  • Map userName to a value that satisfies the userName rules above (for example the sign-in name or mail).
  • Push groups whose names match the mapping table (zeus-os-editors, zeus-os-tenant-acme, ...). Groups with other names are stored but grant nothing.
  • Zeus accepts the common client request shapes: filter=userName eq "..." / externalId eq "..." lookups, PATCH with or without path, string booleans ("True"/"False") for active, member removal by members[value eq "<id>"] or by value list, and PUT of a whole resource.
  • Use the IdP's "test connection" or provisioning log together with GET /ServiceProviderConfig when debugging.

If provisioning fails, the SCIM error body in the IdP's provisioning log states the reason (scimType and detail); a 409 means the user name or externalId already exists, 403 on a user name means it is reserved.

docs.title: Operational notes
docs.text:
• SCIM requires the local user store (ZEUS_OS_LOCAL_USERS_FILE, default data/zeus-os-users.json) to be on persistent storage; if Zeus runs in a mode that does not otherwise initialise it, the first SCIM request creates it (and its break-glass admin, with the usual generated or ZEUS_OS_LOCAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD password).
  • Write operations are serialised in-process; multi-replica deployments must share the data directory (the same requirement as the rest of the local auth store).
  • Manual role edits made through /api/v1/auth/users to a SCIM-managed user are overwritten by the group mapping the next time SCIM changes anything.
  • ZEUS_OS_SCIM_* variables are read per request, so the kill-switch and mapping changes need no restart when set through the process environment; the static token change also takes effect immediately.
  • SCIM requests are not subject to the per-actor API rate limiter; put a reverse-proxy limit in front if the endpoint is internet-reachable.

docs.title: WebAuthn second factor (passkeys / security keys)
docs.text:
Zeus OS can require a WebAuthn credential (a hardware security key or a passkey with user verification) after the password for local logins. It is off by default: with no configuration the login behaves exactly as before and the credential store is never read.

Scope: the built-in local user login (/api/v1/auth/login in local mode, /api/v1/auth/local/login — the break-glass login — in LDAP/SAML/OIDC modes). It does not add a second factor to the IdP-driven SSO/LDAP logins; enforce MFA at the IdP for those.

Code: web/src/webauthn.rs (state machine, credential and challenge stores), web/src/routes/webauthn.rs (HTTP), web/src/local_auth.rs (login gate), ui/src/services/webauthnService.ts, ui/src/stores/authStore.ts, ui/src/components/security/{LoginMfaStep,WebAuthnSettings}.tsx.

docs.title: Enabling
docs.text:
The relying-party identity is deployment specific and is not guessed.

Variable Meaning ZEUS_OS_WEBAUTHN_RP_ID Relying-party ID: the registrable domain the UI is served from, e.g. zeus.example.com. Credentials are bound to it — changing it invalidates every registered key. ZEUS_OS_WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN Exact browser origin(s) of the UI, comma separated, e.g. https://zeus.example.com,https://zeus.example.com:30050. The first is primary. The origin's host must equal or be a subdomain of the RP ID. ZEUS_OS_WEBAUTHN_RP_NAME Optional display name (default Zeus OS). ZEUS_OS_WEBAUTHN_TOTP_RECOVERY Optional, 1 to allow TOTP recovery (see below). Default off.

States:

  • Both unset — disabled. No routes act, login is unchanged.
  • Both set and valid — enabled.
  • Only one set, or invalid — misconfigured: it fails closed. Users who have credentials (or whenever the store cannot be read) get 503 on login instead of a password-only session; users without credentials still log in. The log line webauthn unavailable carries the reason.

Browsers only expose WebAuthn on HTTPS (or localhost), and the origin the browser sees must match ZEUS_OS_WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN exactly, including the port.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
1. Register (Settings → Security → Security keys). The signed-in user re-enters their password, the server issues a registration challenge, the browser prompts for the key, the server verifies and stores the public key. Up to 10 keys per user. User verification (PIN/biometric) is required.
  2. Login. POST /auth/login with a correct password and at least one registered key answers 200: json { "mfa_required": true, "methods": ["webauthn"], "mfa_token": "…", "webauthn": { "publicKey": { … } }, "expires_in": 180 } No session token exists at this point. The client runs navigator.credentials.get() and posts POST /auth/webauthn/login/finish {mfa_token, credential}; only a verified assertion returns the normal login body (token, role, …).
  3. Users with no registered key get the normal session straight after the password.

Security properties:

  • Challenges are server side, in memory only, single use, expire after 180 s, and are bound to the user and the ceremony kind (a registration challenge cannot complete a login and vice versa; another user cannot complete yours). mfa_token is 256 random bits. At most 4096 ceremonies are pending at once.
  • User verification is required; the sign counter is checked and a regression (possible cloned key) rejects the login and writes webauthn_clone_suspected. The updated counter is persisted before the session is issued — if that write fails, login fails.
  • Every verification attempt consumes its mfa_token; after a failure the user starts again from the password step. Failed assertions/registrations count against the login rate limiter (key webauthn:<user>, 10 failures / 15 min, then 429), separate from the password counter.
  • Adding or removing a key requires the account password again (a stolen session cannot silently add a persistent second factor).
  • Only public keys, credential ids, sign counters and labels are stored: <ZEUS_OS_DATA_DIR>/webauthn-credentials.json, mode 0600, atomically replaced. A missing file means "no keys"; an unreadable/corrupt file is an error (login fails closed) and the file is left untouched. Challenges and credential bodies are never logged.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Public (complete a password login): POST /api/v1/auth/webauthn/login/finish, POST /api/v1/auth/webauthn/login/recover.

Authenticated (Authorization: Bearer): GET /api/v1/auth/webauthn/status, POST /api/v1/auth/webauthn/register/start {label, password}, POST /api/v1/auth/webauthn/register/finish {credential}, POST /api/v1/auth/webauthn/credentials/{id}/remove {password}, DELETE /api/v1/auth/webauthn/users/{username}/credentials (admin only).

These routes are deliberately outside the viewer write-block so every role can manage its own keys; each handler acts only on the caller's own subject, and the admin reset does an exact role == "admin" check itself.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
• Another registered key. Register at least two keys.
  • Admin reset (always available): an admin calls DELETE /api/v1/auth/webauthn/users/{username}/credentials. The user can then log in with the password alone and re-register. Audited as webauthn_admin_reset (subject = admin, detail = target and count).
  • TOTP (opt-in): with ZEUS_OS_WEBAUTHN_TOTP_RECOVERY=1 the mfa_required answer also lists "totp", and POST /auth/webauthn/login/recover {mfa_token, code} accepts a code from the user's existing authenticator enrolment (/auth/mfa/*, secrets in the zeus-os-mfa-secrets Kubernetes Secret). This is a weaker path than a key; leave it off if you want phishing-resistant MFA only. Audited as webauthn_recovery_totp. (Today TOTP is otherwise only used for console step-up, not at login.)
  • Locked out with no admin left. Stop the server, delete the user's entry from webauthn-credentials.json (or the whole file) or unset ZEUS_OS_WEBAUTHN_RP_ID/_ORIGIN to disable the feature, and restart. Deleting a local user also removes their keys.

docs.title: Audit events (auth-audit.jsonl, SIEM as auth.<event>)
docs.text: login_mfa_required, login_mfa_unavailable, webauthn_register, webauthn_register_failure, webauthn_remove, webauthn_login_success, webauthn_login_failure, webauthn_clone_suspected, webauthn_locked_out, webauthn_reauth_failure, webauthn_admin_reset, webauthn_admin_reset_denied, webauthn_recovery_totp, webauthn_recovery_failure, plus the normal login (detail local+webauthn or local+totp-recovery).

docs.title: Operational notes
docs.text:
• Challenge state lives in the process. Run one replica (or sticky sessions) for the login/registration ceremonies; a restart between the two steps just makes the user retry.
  • The credential file is per data directory; back it up with the rest of ZEUS_OS_DATA_DIR.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Automated (no browser, no server): cargo test -p zeus-os-web --bins webauthn uses webauthn-authenticator-rs's software passkey as a virtual authenticator against the real ceremony code and the real login/finish handlers, covering the password → mfa_required → session state machine, single-use/TTL challenges, clone detection, rate limiting, fail-closed store handling and the disabled default. UI: cd ui && npx vitest run src/services/webauthnService.test.ts src/stores/authStoreMfa.test.ts src/components/security.

Manual browser check with a virtual authenticator (not automated in CI because it needs a running server and a matching RP ID/origin):

  1. ZEUS_OS_WEBAUTHN_RP_ID=localhost ZEUS_OS_WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5050 cargo run -p zeus-os-web (serve the built UI, or use the Vite dev server with origin http://localhost:3000 added to the comma list).
  2. In Chrome DevTools → three-dot menu → More tools → WebAuthn, tick Enable virtual authenticator environment, add an authenticator: protocol ctap2, transport internal (or usb), tick Supports user verification and Automatic presence simulation / Set user verified. With Playwright/CDP the equivalent is WebAuthn.enable + WebAuthn.addVirtualAuthenticator {protocol:'ctap2', transport:'internal', hasUserVerification:true, isUserVerified:true, automaticPresenceSimulation:true}.
  3. Sign in as admin, open Settings → Security → Security keys, add a key (the virtual authenticator answers automatically), sign out, sign in again: after the password the Use security key step appears and completes with the virtual authenticator. Remove the authenticator in DevTools and confirm the login step then cannot be completed (recover via admin reset).

docs.title: zeus-os-cli
docs.text:
Headless command-line tool built on the same Rust library as the TUI and web server.

cargo build --release -p zeus-os-cli      # binary: zeus-os-cli

There are two kinds of commands.

Kind Commands Talks to Auth Direct vm, snapshot, node, storage, guest the cluster, via your kubeconfig your kubeconfig RBAC REST backup, template, network, tenant a running zeus-os-web (--server) bearer token; tenancy, RBAC and audit apply

Every listing command accepts -o table|json|yaml (default table). json/yaml emit the full objects; table is a summary view.

docs.title: Direct commands
docs.text:
Namespaced commands take -n/--namespace (default default; listings default to all namespaces).

zeus-os-cli vm list -n prod -o json
zeus-os-cli vm get web -n prod -o yaml
zeus-os-cli vm start|stop|restart web -n prod
zeus-os-cli vm pause|unpause|softreboot web -n prod       # need a running VMI
zeus-os-cli vm reset web -n prod --yes                    # hard reset (no guest flush)
zeus-os-cli vm clone web web-copy -n prod                 # same namespace, created stopped
zeus-os-cli vm migrate web -n prod                        # live migration; refuses if LiveMigratable=False
zeus-os-cli vm delete web -n prod --yes

zeus-os-cli vm templates                                  # local templates (~/.zeus-os/templates.json or built-ins)
zeus-os-cli vm create --template "Ubuntu 24.04 LTS" --name web -n prod
zeus-os-cli vm create -f vm.yaml -n prod                  # -f - reads stdin; -n must match metadata.namespace if set

zeus-os-cli vm console web -n prod                        # prints connection info only
zeus-os-cli vm vnc web -n prod --server https://zeus:30050

vm console / vm vnc do not open a session or spawn a viewer. They confirm the VMI exists and print the KubeVirt subresource path (a WebSocket upgrade endpoint on the Kubernetes API server) and, for VNC with --server, the Zeus web console URL.

zeus-os-cli snapshot list -n prod
zeus-os-cli snapshot create web -n prod --name pre-upgrade --quiesce
zeus-os-cli snapshot restore pre-upgrade --vm web -n prod --yes   # replaces the VM's disks
zeus-os-cli snapshot delete pre-upgrade -n prod --yes

zeus-os-cli node list
zeus-os-cli node cordon worker-1          # AFFECTS SCHEDULING: no new workloads land on it
zeus-os-cli node uncordon worker-1
zeus-os-cli node drain worker-1 --yes     # cordon + live-migrate KubeVirt VMs off the node

zeus-os-cli storage pvc list -n prod -o json
zeus-os-cli guest status web -n prod

node drain cordons the node and starts live migrations for the KubeVirt VMs running on it. It does not evict ordinary pods, and the node stays cordoned afterwards (run node uncordon). If some VMs cannot be migrated the command lists them and exits non-zero.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Destructive commands (vm delete, vm reset, snapshot restore, snapshot delete, node drain) require --yes. On a terminal without --yes you get a y/N prompt; with stdin not a terminal (scripts, CI) they refuse.
  • The referenced VM/VMI/snapshot/node is verified to exist before anything is changed, and names are validated as Kubernetes names.
  • Restoring a snapshot requires the snapshot to be readyToUse.

docs.title: REST commands
docs.text:
export ZEUS_OS_SERVER=https://zeus.example.com:30050
export ZEUS_OS_TOKEN=v9s_...              # preferred over --token (visible in `ps`)

zeus-os-cli backup list
zeus-os-cli backup create nightly -n prod -n dev --ttl-hours 168
zeus-os-cli backup restores
zeus-os-cli backup restore nightly --map prod=prod-copy
zeus-os-cli template list
zeus-os-cli template get small-linux -n zeus      # -n only needed if the name exists in several namespaces
zeus-os-cli network policies list -n prod
zeus-os-cli network attachments list
zeus-os-cli tenant list -o json
Flag Env Purpose --server <url> ZEUS_OS_SERVER Zeus web URL (a trailing / or /api/v1 is tolerated) --token <token> ZEUS_OS_TOKEN Bearer token --insecure ZEUS_OS_INSECURE Skip TLS verification (self-signed lab clusters only; warns on use) --timeout <secs> Per-request timeout, default 30

Routes used: GET/POST /api/v1/velero/backups, GET/POST /api/v1/velero/restores, GET /api/v1/vm-templates, GET /api/v1/networkpolicies, GET /api/v1/network-attachments, GET /api/v1/tenancy/tenants. template get filters the list client-side (the server has no single-template route). backup restore checks the backup is visible before creating the restore.

docs.title: Tokens: use scoped v9s_* tokens
docs.text: An API token with an empty scope list is unrestricted: it can do everything its role allows. For automation create a v9s_* token with explicit scopes (for example read for the listing commands) and, where possible, a tenant-limited role. The create/restore commands need a token that permits writes.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Errors are printed as Error: ... and exit 1. HTTP failures are mapped to actionable text: 401 (missing/invalid token), 403 (role/tenant/scope denies the operation), 404, 429, other 5xx, plus connection, TLS and timeout failures naming the server URL.

docs.title: The zeus-os-client crate
docs.text: client/ is a small typed HTTP client (ApiClient, ClientConfig, ClientError) for /api/v1, usable from other Rust tools. TLS verification is on unless insecure is set, the token is never printed in Debug output, and path segments are validated before interpolation.

docs.title: Zeus OS REST API reference (OpenAPI)
docs.text: The API is described by an OpenAPI 3.0.3 document, served live at GET /api/v1/openapi.json (Swagger UI at /api/v1/docs) and checked in as docs/openapi.json. The typed Python and Go SDKs (sdk/README.md) are generated from that file.

docs.title: How trustworthy is a schema?
docs.text:
Nothing in the spec is hand-typed from memory. The bulk of it is derived from the server's own code:

  • the route table (.route("/path", get(h).post(h2)) registrations under web/src/),
  • each handler's signature: Path<..>, Query<T>, Json<T> request bodies, Result<Json<T>, _> / Json<T> responses,
  • the serde definition of every referenced struct/enum (rename, rename_all, default, skip_serializing_if, flatten, untagged enums, generics such as PaginatedResponse<T>).

Every operation says how deep that goes in x-zeus-schema:

x-zeus-schema Meaning typed a request and/or response schema was derived from Rust types untyped the handler was analysed but its body is serde_json::Value (free-form JSON) or unknown none the handler could not be resolved (e.g. a closure): method and path only curated hand-written operation (only for routes with no derived operation)

Other extensions: x-zeus-role (minimum role the handler itself enforces: authenticated, editor, admin) and x-zeus-source (handler that produced the operation). Independently of x-zeus-role, viewers are denied every POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE, and namespaced resources are filtered by tenant.

Known limits, so you do not over-trust the spec:

  • A success response that a handler builds with json!({...}) is untyped; the field list is not inferred.
  • (StatusCode, Json<T>) returns are documented as 2XX (the exact code is not knowable from the type).
  • Types that live outside this repository (Kubernetes objects, ...) are free-form JSON with a description saying so.
  • An Option<T> field is nullable and not required (Rust may emit null, or omit it via skip_serializing_if).
  • Enums with data-carrying variants are free-form; untagged enums of newtype variants become oneOf.
  • Routes registered per auth mode (/auth/login) document the union; see the operation description.
  • WebSocket routes (/ws/...) are not REST and are not in the spec. /health and /ready live at the server root and carry a path-level servers override.

docs.title: Authentication in the spec
docs.text: Three security schemes, all carrying the same token: bearerAuth (Authorization: Bearer <token>, preferred), cookieAuth (zeus_os_token cookie) and queryToken (?zeus_os_token=, for iframe embeds; URLs get logged). A token is a session token from login/OIDC/SAML, a per-user API token (v9s_...) or the deployment ZEUS_OS_API_KEY. Public endpoints (/auth/config, the login endpoints, /health, /ready) declare security: []. Every other operation lists a 401 response; errors are {"error": "<message>"} (components/schemas/Error).

docs.title: Layers and files
docs.text:
Layer File Edited by Derived operations + schemas web/src/routes/openapi/generated.json python3 scripts/gen-openapi-paths.py --update (never by hand) Curated summaries/tags web/src/routes/openapi/curated.rs by hand; only for real routes (unit test enforces it) Auth/health overlays web/src/routes/openapi/overlays.rs by hand; replaces derived bodies/responses Assembly + tests web/src/routes/openapi.rs by hand Served/checked-in rendering docs/openapi.json ZEUS_OS_WRITE_OPENAPI=1 cargo test -p zeus-os-web --bins openapi_json_matches_checked_in_docs Route inventory + coverage docs/openapi-paths.json, scripts/openapi-coverage-baseline.json python3 scripts/gen-openapi-paths.py [--update]

Curated entries only fill gaps: a curated summary/description/tag wins, but a curated generic {"type":"object"} body never replaces a derived typed schema.

docs.title: Regenerating after you add or change a route
docs.text:
python3 scripts/gen-openapi-paths.py --update     # 1. re-derive generated.json, refresh baseline + route inventory
ZEUS_OS_WRITE_OPENAPI=1 cargo test -p zeus-os-web --bins openapi_json_matches_checked_in_docs   # 2. docs/openapi.json
python3 scripts/gen-sdks.py                       # 3. SDKs
python3 scripts/gen-openapi-paths.py --check && python3 scripts/gen-sdks.py --check   # verify (CI)
cargo test -p zeus-os-web --bins openapi          # spec validity tests

--check fails if documented/typed coverage fell below scripts/openapi-coverage-baseline.json or if generated.json is stale relative to the Rust sources. The openapi Rust tests fail if docs/openapi.json is stale.

If a handler you add is untyped, give it a concrete Json<YourStruct> return type (with Serialize) rather than Json<Value>; that is the whole trick to a typed spec and typed SDKs.

docs.title: What the Rust tests check
docs.text: cargo test -p zeus-os-web --bins openapi validates the served document: OpenAPI 3.0.3 structure, every $ref resolves, every {param} in a path is declared as a required path parameter (and no undeclared ones), every operationId is a unique identifier, no two paths are equivalent templates, every status key is valid, every security requirement names a defined scheme, every curated overlay describes a real route, and docs/openapi.json equals the served spec.

docs.title: Using the API directly
docs.text:
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:5050/api/v1/auth/login -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"admin","password":"..."}' | jq -r .token)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 'http://localhost:5050/api/v1/vms?page=1&per_page=20'
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:5050/api/v1/vms/prod/web-1/start

Generate a client in another language with any OpenAPI 3.0 generator pointed at docs/openapi.json; operation ids are snake_case handler names (they change only if a handler is renamed).

Zeus OS is the visual day-2 control plane for KubeVirt virtual machines and Kubernetes infrastructure. This package is written for operators, platform admins, and FinOps users — not application developers hacking on the source tree.

docs.title: Admin Basics (Customer Deployments)
docs.text:
Platform-facing configuration for Zeus OS. Operators using the UI day-to-day can skip this unless asked to verify URL, TLS, or auth.

For the full env-var and production checklist, see Handbook — Administration & Configuration.

docs.title: Ports customers care about
docs.text:
Port Service Typical use 5050 zeus-os-web Direct / local dashboard + API 30050 NodePort (common deploy) Cluster-exposed HTTPS dashboard 8081 Optional console-proxy Sidecar console proxy 9191 / 9443 PacketWolf Network intelligence (proxied) 9090 Prometheus Metrics source (cluster)

Zeus itself listens on 5050 (plus optional console proxy). Give customers the ingress or NodePort URL, not internal ClusterIP addresses.

docs.title: Fastest production-style deploy
docs.text:
# On a machine with kubeconfig + KubeVirt already installed
./scripts/deploy-remote.sh <HOST> <SSH_USER> --k3s
# → https://<HOST>:30050

Air-gapped: AIR_GAPPED_INSTALL.md. Helm profiles: HELM_VALUES_PROFILES.md.

docs.title: From a binary bundle (no git clone, no build tools)
docs.text:
If you received a zeus-os-<version>-linux-amd64.tar.gz bundle (built via scripts/package-binary-remote.sh), it ships the Helm chart plus a script that builds a runtime image from the bundle's own binaries — no source tree, no cargo/npm:

tar xzf zeus-os-*-linux-amd64.tar.gz && cd zeus-os-*-linux-amd64
./install-cluster.sh                                          # KubeVirt/CDI/Cilium prereqs
./install-to-kubernetes.sh --registry <your-registry>/zeus-os --push
./apply-cluster-network.sh

install-to-kubernetes.sh --help shows namespace/release/dry-run options, and a local single-node cluster (kind/k3s/minikube) sharing the build daemon's image store can skip --push entirely. Note: an image built this way lacks the helm CLI the full-source web/Dockerfile bundles — the in-app /helm repo/install UI won't work; use web/Dockerfile instead if you need it. Browser-VNC assets and GuestKit agent binaries are included.

docs.title: Authentication (what to enable)
docs.text:
Resolution order on the server:

  1. ZEUS_OS_NO_AUTH=1 — lab only
  2. ZEUS_OS_API_KEY — static bearer for API
  3. ZEUS_OS_AUTH=local|ldap|saml|oidc — interactive login

Enterprise detail: ENTERPRISE_AUTH_TENANCY.md.

When ldap/saml/oidc is set, the local admin account stays available as a break-glass fallback automatically — the login screen shows an explicit toggle to pick between the directory/ SSO method and the local admin account, rather than requiring the operator to know a hidden URL.

Tell operators:

  • Dashboard URL + auth method
  • Whether MFA / SSO is required
  • That RDP/SSH use guest credentials

docs.title: Local admin password
docs.text:
The built-in local admin account defaults to Admin@321 when ZEUS_OS_LOCAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD isn't set — change this before any internet-facing or production install.

The default differs by install path:

Install path Default behavior Helm chart Fixed Admin@321 unless config.localAuth.adminPassword or config.localAuth.adminPasswordSecretRef is set in values.yaml Binary bundle (scripts/package-binary-remote.sh) Generates a random strong password automatically unless ZEUS_OS_LOCAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD is set in the bundle's env file — does not fall back to Admin@321

Set your own password at install time (Helm):

helm upgrade --install zeus-os ./chart --set config.localAuth.adminPassword="a-real-password"
# or reference an existing Secret instead of inlining the password:
# --set config.localAuth.adminPasswordSecretRef.name=zeus-os-local-auth

docs.title: TLS (required for browser VNC)
docs.text:
export ZEUS_OS_TLS_CERT=/path/to/cert.pem
export ZEUS_OS_TLS_KEY=/path/to/key.pem
# or terminate TLS at ingress and serve the SPA behind HTTPS

Without a secure context, in-browser VNC will not work; serial console still can.

docs.title: Enterprise SSO / OIDC (Keycloak)
docs.text:
How to sign into Zeus OS with a real identity provider — Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, or any standards-compliant OIDC IdP — after install.

Zeus OS's OIDC relying-party implementation is generic (discovery + JWKS + RS256/384/512 signature validation) and needs zero code changes for any real IdP. Verified end-to-end live against a real Keycloak realm.

Unlike some products in the suite, Zeus OS does not bundle a Keycloak instance in its Helm chart — you point it at a Keycloak (or other OIDC provider) you already have, or stand one up separately. Whichever SSO mode is active, the built-in local admin account (admin / Admin@321 by default) stays available underneath it automatically as a break-glass fallback — the login screen shows a toggle between the two, not a hidden URL.

docs.title: Option A — Bring your own OIDC provider (Keycloak example)
docs.text:
1. Create a realm and client in Keycloak. Confidential client. Valid Redirect URI must be the real backend callback:

text https://<zeus-host>:30050/api/v1/auth/oidc/callback

Not /auth/callback — that's a different, frontend-only route the backend redirects the browser to after it has already validated the token server-side (carrying ?token=, not an OAuth code/state pair). Registering the frontend route as the IdP redirect_uri breaks the flow silently — no error until the callback lands on the wrong page.

  1. Add a Group Membership protocol mapper on the client's dedicated scope (Token Claim Name = groups by default, configurable via ZEUS_OS_OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM; turn Full group path off, so the claim contains bare names like zeus-os-admins, not /zeus-os-admins). This mapper is included in every token issued to the client automatically — don't add groups to the requested OAuth scopes (see the gotcha below).

  2. If Keycloak is fronted by plain HTTP (no TLS termination), its default sslRequired=external will reject every OIDC endpoint — including /.well-known/openid-configuration — with a generic HTTPS required error that has nothing to do with your Zeus OS config. Set the realm's Require SSL → None (Realm settings → General) for a lab/demo setup, or put real TLS in front of Keycloak for production.

  3. Deploy Zeus OS pointed at it:

bash cp contrib/zyvorai-oidc-keycloak.env.example my-oidc.env # edit issuer/client-id for your realm set -a && source my-oidc.env && set +a ZEUS_OS_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET='<secret from Keycloak Credentials tab>' \ ./scripts/deploy-remote.sh <HOST> <SSH_USER> --with-oidc

--with-oidc writes a Helm values file (not --set, since client secrets can contain characters --set mishandles) setting config.authMode: oidc and the full config.oidc.* block, including groupAdmin/groupEditor for role mapping. It survives the next helm upgrade since deploys always pass --reuse-values.

  1. Verify: GET /api/v1/auth/config should return mode: "oidc", localFallback: true, and an oidc block echoing your issuer/client-id/redirect-uri. Then a real browser login — click Continue with OpenID Connect on the sign-in screen.

Manual env-var reference (no deploy script): Enterprise auth & tenancy links to the full ENTERPRISE_AUTH_TENANCY.md table (ZEUS_OS_AUTH=oidc, ZEUS_OS_OIDC_ISSUER, ZEUS_OS_OIDC_CLIENT_ID, ZEUS_OS_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET, ZEUS_OS_OIDC_REDIRECT_URI, ZEUS_OS_OIDC_SCOPES, ZEUS_OS_OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM, ZEUS_OS_OIDC_GROUP_ADMIN, ZEUS_OS_OIDC_GROUP_EDITOR).

docs.title: Option B — LDAP / Active Directory instead
docs.text: Zeus OS also speaks LDAP directly (ZEUS_OS_AUTH=ldap) if your organization uses Active Directory rather than an OIDC IdP — see Admin basics for the resolution order and ENTERPRISE_AUTH_TENANCY.md for the LDAP variable table. Local admin stays available as break-glass here too.

docs.title: Option C — Local admin only (no IdP)
docs.text: Leave ZEUS_OS_AUTH unset (the default). Sign in with the local admin account — change Admin@321 before any internet-facing install (config.localAuth.adminPassword in Helm, or reference a Secret via config.localAuth.adminPasswordSecretRef). See Admin basics — Local admin password.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix {"error":"invalid_request","error_description":"HTTPS required"} from Keycloak Realm's sslRequired=external rejecting a plain-HTTP request Set Require SSL → None on the realm (lab), or put real TLS in front of Keycloak invalid_scope: Invalid scopes: ... groups groups (or another claim name) added to ZEUS_OS_OIDC_SCOPES Remove it — openid,profile,email is enough; the group mapper applies regardless of requested scope Redirects back but lands on the wrong page / generic error Client's redirect_uri is /auth/callback instead of /api/v1/auth/oidc/callback Fix the Valid Redirect URI in the IdP client to the real backend path Logged in but role is always Viewer Group claim not reaching the token, or group names don't match ZEUS_OS_OIDC_GROUP_ADMIN/GROUP_EDITOR Use the IdP's token-evaluate/preview tool to confirm the groups claim is present and matches; check "Full group path" is off Local admin missing from the login screen Should not happen — it's automatic whenever an SSO mode is active Check GET /api/v1/auth/config reports localFallback: true; file a bug if not

docs.title: Getting Started with Zeus OS
docs.text: This guide gets a customer from “I have a URL” to first useful work in the web dashboard.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Requirement Notes Kubernetes cluster with KubeVirt installed Zeus is day-2 ops — it does not bootstrap the cluster Reachable Zeus OS URL Often https://<host>:30050 (NodePort) or https://<host>:5050 Login credentials Provided by your platform admin (local / LDAP / SAML / OIDC) Browser Modern Chromium, Firefox, or Safari. HTTPS required for in-browser VNC

Optional: kubectl access is not required for normal UI work.

docs.title: 1. Open the dashboard
docs.text:
1. Open the URL your admin shared (example: https://cluster.example:30050).
  2. If the browser warns about a self-signed certificate, confirm with your admin, then proceed (or install the org CA).
  3. You should land on login, or directly on Home (/) if auth is disabled in a lab.

Common mistake: Port 5092 is GuestKit / Machina territory on some Zyvor stacks — not Zeus OS. Prefer the URL that ends in the Zeus NodePort (often 30050) or the documented ingress host.

docs.title: 2. Sign in
docs.text:
Auth depends on how the deployment is configured:

Mode What you do Local users Username + password from your admin LDAP / Active Directory Corporate directory credentials SAML / OIDC “Sign in with …” → identity provider Lab only ZEUS_OS_NO_AUTH — no login (never use in production)

API automation uses bearer tokens / API keys from Settings → API access or Identity Center — not the guest OS password.

Windows RDP prompts for the guest credentials, not your Zeus login.

docs.title: 3. Orient yourself (60 seconds)
docs.text:
1. Home (/) — chapter pulse, Get the highlights, and teaser into Attention, VMs, Health.
  2. Attention (/attention) — ranked actions, Issue Stream, and day-2 activity when Home shows warnings.
  3. Sidebar / Finder — centers such as VMs, Storage, Monitoring, Settings.
  4. Command palette — open with the keyboard shortcut shown in the shell (typically ⌘K / Ctrl+K) and type a page name.
  5. Browse vs workbench — inventory lists are safe to explore; power actions live on the VM workbench so production VMs are harder to disrupt by accident.
  6. Getting started checklist — first-time visitors see a banner on Home; click Getting started checklist (or Help → Getting Started) for a short, role-aware task list (admins get cluster/team setup, everyone else gets "find/create a VM", "open a console", "check cost"). Progress is saved to your account, so it follows you across devices and browsers — not just this one tab.

See Using the Dashboard for navigation details.

docs.title: A. Browse and power a VM
docs.text:
1. Go to VMs → /vms.
  2. Filter by namespace or name.
  3. Open a VM → /vms/<namespace>/<name> (workbench).
  4. Use Start / Stop / Restart / Pause as needed.
  5. Confirm status updates in the inventory.

Guide: Virtual Machines

docs.title: B. Open a live console
docs.text:
1. From a Running VM workbench, open Console → VNC (graphical) or Serial (text).
  2. VNC needs HTTPS. If the session is black, click Focus in the console toolbar.
  3. For RDP/SSH: use Remote access to expose a NodePort, then connect with your OS client (downloadable .rdp or ssh command). VNC remains the in-browser default.

Guide: Consoles & remote access

docs.title: C. Create a VM
docs.text:
1. Open VM setup → /vm-setup (or /vms/new).
  2. Choose instance type / preference / template (or AI-assisted manifest if enabled).
  3. For Windows: if Settings → Network shows Kryton Connected, prefer the Kryton catalog path (template IDs like windows-11-enterprise). Otherwise use Autounattend / ISO.
  4. Review disks, network, and namespace.
  5. Deploy — the VM appears under /vms (Kryton creates deep-link via providerRef).

Guides: Create a machine · Windows via Kryton

docs.title: D. Snapshot and restore
docs.text:
1. Snapshot Manager → /snapshot-manager — take an on-demand or scheduled snapshot.
  2. To recover: Restore Wizard → /restore-wizard and follow the guided restore.

Guide: Snapshots

docs.title: E. Cost check and rightsizing
docs.text:
1. Cost Intelligence → /cost-intelligence — spend by VM / namespace.
  2. Rightsizing → /rightsizing — idle / oversized recommendations.

Guide: Cost Intelligence

docs.title: 5. Optional: TUI and CLI
docs.text:
Same cluster, different surfaces:

# Terminal UI (k9s-style)
zeus-os
zeus-os production    # namespace filter

# Headless CLI (examples depend on install path)
zeus-os-cli --help

API: /api/v1 on the same host as the dashboard. OpenAPI lives under Developer Center / API Docs (/api-docs).

docs.title: Browse vs workbench (important)
docs.text:
Zeus separates inventory from actions:

  • Browse (/vms, /pods, /nodes, …) — read, filter, compare, open details.
  • Workbench (/vms/:namespace/:name, hardware studio, consoles) — start/stop, hot-plug, remote access, guest agent.

That design reduces accidental power actions on production fleets.

docs.title: Finding any page
docs.text:
1. Sidebar section (Core, Cluster, Observe, Run, Security, Cost, More).
  2. Command palette — type “packetwolf”, “velero”, “cost”, etc.

  4. Favorites (/favorites) — pin pages you use daily.

Every page guide includes Operate from the console (UX) — concrete clicks after you land on the route.

docs.title: Namespaces and tenancy
docs.text:
Lists usually respect the active namespace filter (and tenant scope if multi-tenancy is enabled). If a VM “disappeared”:

  1. Clear or broaden the namespace filter.
  2. Confirm you are in the correct tenant (Identity / Tenancy).
  3. Refresh — live watches may lag briefly after create/delete.

docs.title: Page-by-page guides
docs.text:
Each guide follows the same shape:

  1. Purpose — what this screen is for
  2. When to use it — typical jobs
  3. How to get there — route and nav path
  4. Operate from the console (UX) — concrete clicks after you land
